author: reek
body: The direction bit is checked at runtime by the compiler's default FileSystem servicer (emit-fs-write-servicer-helper, X86_64Helpers): it tests cap-filesystem-write before it elevates, and jumps past the whole elevate-call-lower sequence when the bit is clear. Until now that jump was inspection-verified only. codex/test/fs-servicer exercises the pass path and nothing exercised the refusal, because the obvious way to reach it cannot be written: a program declaring [FileSystem.Read] that calls write-file is rejected at compile time, so the source that would reach the branch never becomes a binary.

author: reek
body: The way in is to hold the row and lose the bit. This program declares both directions, so it compiles and boots with both granted -- and then drops cap-filesystem-write out of its own process-table entry with process-restrict-cap, which is what [Capability] is for. The second write is made by the same code, against the same disk, one bit apart from the first.

author: reek
body: Reporting both writes is the discipline this battery already runs on. A test that showed only the refusal would print the same thing whether the bit was honoured or writes were broken outright, and a failure for the wrong reason reads exactly like a pass:

author: reek
body: The last line is the one that makes the refusal real rather than merely reported. A servicer that returned False and elevated anyway would print the same "denied write False" and leave the bytes on the disk. Only reading back distinguishes a write that was refused from a write that landed and lied about it.

author: reek
body: That read is of a SECOND file, and the reason is a trap this test fell into first. The denied write originally overwrote OK.TXT and the check was that it still said "hello". It does -- but it says "hello" with the write bit intact as well, because fat16-write-file answers True to a rewrite of an existing name without changing its contents. The check could not fail and would have shipped reading as proof. Writing OK2.TXT makes absence the evidence: a refused write leaves nothing to read, and an admitted one leaves "second" behind. Both are in scope under the "OK" prefix, so the grant is not what separates them.

author: reek
body: The read after the drop is the second control: the restrict has to be surgical. FileSystem.Read is a separate bit and was never dropped, so a machine that answers the read is attenuating the grant, and one that refuses it revoked the family. Denying what was legitimately asked for is not enforcement.

author: reek
body: No Device.Block anywhere, on purpose. The servicer's elevation is what reaches the disk, so this also holds the fs-servicer guarantee steady across the drop: the elevation is gated by the direction bit and not a door beside it.
